items.answer: ATT = mean(treated outcomes) - mean(matched control outcomes) = (30000+35000+40000+45000)/4 - (25000+28000+32000+38000)/4 = 37500 - 30750 = 6750 dollars. Propensity score matching is preferred over exact matching with many covariates because: (1) exact matching suffers from the curse of dimensionality - with k binary covariates there are 2^k possible strata, many of which may be empty; (2) propensity scores reduce the matching problem to a single dimension while still balancing all observed covariates; (3) it allows matches between treated and control units that are similar on their overall probability of treatment even if they differ on individual covariates.

prompt.content: You are an expert in causal inference and experimental design. Answer precisely with mathematical rigor when appropriate.

A researcher uses propensity score matching to estimate the causal effect of a job training program on wages. The propensity scores for treated units are [0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9] and for control units are [0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75]. The treated outcomes are [30000, 35000, 40000, 45000] and matched control outcomes are [25000, 28000, 32000, 38000]. Calculate the ATT, and explain why propensity score matching is preferred over exact matching when there are many covariates.

items.answer: Conditioning on Z blocks the backdoor path because Z is the only non-causal path from X to Y. By holding Z constant, we break the spurious association between X and Y through Z, leaving only the direct causal path X -> Y. This satisfies the backdoor criterion. If we condition on a collider (a variable caused by both X and Y, e.g., C <- X, C <- Y, X -> Y), we OPEN a spurious path between X and Y, creating a non-causal association. This is collider bias (Berkson's paradox) and can make uncorrelated variables appear correlated.

prompt.content: You are an expert in causal inference and experimental design. Answer precisely with mathematical rigor when appropriate.

Given a causal DAG where Z is a confounder (Z -> X, Z -> Y, X -> Y), explain why conditioning on Z blocks the backdoor path X <- Z -> Y and produces an unbiased estimate of the causal effect of X on Y. Then explain what happens if we mistakenly condition on a collider instead of a confounder.
